name: Cancel a pending order
description: Applies when a customer asks to cancel an existing order; the order must be verified against the cancellation policy, including the membership-tier cancellation threshold, before being cancelled and refunded.
procedure:
- Authenticate the customer and fetch the order details.
- Verify the order status is **pending**; refuse for processed, delivered, or already cancelled orders.
- Verify the cancellation reason is "no longer needed" or "ordered by mistake".
- Look up the customer's membership tier and compare the order total (sum of item prices) against the tier's cancellation limit: bronze **$200**, silver **$300**, gold **$500**. A run confirmed that a pending order above the bronze limit of $200 could not be cancelled even though a documented threshold might suggest otherwise, so always apply the tier limit before agreeing.
- If over the limit, refuse with reason over_threshold; otherwise cancel the order and refund the payment to the payment method(s) used.
- Cancellation is free of charge.
check: Recompute the order total from the item prices in the order details and compare it against the customer's tier limit from the policy before deciding to cancel or refuse.
known_bad: Cancelling a pending order whose item prices sum to more than the customer's membership-tier limit (e.g. a $450 order for a bronze member) — the recomputed total exceeds the tier's threshold, so the cancellation must be refused instead.

name: Modify items on a pending order
description: Applies when a customer asks to change or swap an item on an existing order for a different variant of the same product, regardless of the word the customer uses; the order status must be checked first to decide between a modification (pending) and an exchange (delivered).
procedure:
- Authenticate the customer by name and zip, then fetch the order and read its status.
- Route by status: a pending order is modified with the modification tool; a delivered order is an exchange (customers often say "modify" for a delivered order), so follow the exchange procedure instead.
- Look up the product's variants: confirm the requested replacement is the same product, is available, and is not clearance.
- Compute the price difference as the new variant price minus the current item price, and confirm the customer has approved a payment method on file that covers it.
- Submit the modification or exchange with the correct item IDs and payment method, then read the returned order to confirm the status and recorded price difference.
check: Recompute the price difference from the variant prices in the product data, and confirm the tool used matches the order status (modification only for pending, exchange for delivered); a status of 'exchange requested' on what was submitted as a modification, or a mismatched difference, means the wrong operation or amount was used.
known_bad: Charging the absolute value of the price difference when the replacement is cheaper than the original item, so the customer is billed instead of refunded; the recomputed signed difference will not match the amount on the returned order.

name: Process a customer return request
description: Applies when a customer asks to return items from a delivered order; eligibility (delivery status, return window by product category, clearance status, valid reason) must be verified and the restocking-fee-adjusted refund computed before registering the return.
procedure:
- Authenticate the customer, fetch the order, and confirm the order is delivered and the items belong to it.
- Verify the reason is one of the accepted reasons (e.g. defective, no longer needed, wrong item).
- Look up the product's category to get the return window in days after delivery, and confirm the item is not a clearance final sale; refuse if outside the window or clearance.
- Apply the restocking fee for the customer's membership tier (a percentage withheld from the item price).
- Compute the refund as item price minus the fee, truncating to cents (drop extra decimals); do not round up.
- Refund to a gift card on the customer's account is always an accepted destination; register the return, which issues the refund.
check: Recompute the refund independently as floor(price × (1 − fee_rate) × 100) / 100 and confirm it equals the refund amount recorded by the system in the payment history; if the system's amount is lower than a rounded computation, trust the system (truncation) and report that amount.
known_bad: On a return of an item priced at 99.99 for a membership tier with a 15% restocking fee, a rounded computation gives 84.99, but the correct truncating result is 84.99; for a price where the fee produces a third decimal of 5 or more, such as 125.00 at 15% (106.25 exactly, or a case like 62.50 at 15% = 53.125), trusting a rounded-up value of 53.13 fails because the system records the truncated 53.12.

name: Count days to a window limit
description: Applies when a return, exchange, or cancellation decision hinges on whether the days elapsed since delivery (or placement) exceed a policy window, especially when the count lands near the limit.
procedure:
- Take the start date from the order record itself (delivered_at for returns and exchanges, placed_at for cancellations), not from the customer's wording.
- Count elapsed days by walking month by month and using each month's real length; do not assume every month has 30 or 31 days.
- Compare the elapsed count against the documented window for the product category; refuse only if the count is strictly greater than the limit.
- When the count is close to the limit, recount before refusing or accepting; an off-by-one or wrong month length changes the decision.
check: Recompute the elapsed days a second way, e.g. day-of-year arithmetic ((day-of-year of today) minus (day-of-year of the start date), adjusted for a year rollover), and confirm it matches the month-by-month count before acting on the decision.
known_bad: Counting a delivery on May 1 with today June 1 as 30 elapsed days because 'one month' has passed; the recount gives 31, so a 30-day window is already expired rather than just met — the check exposes the wrong month length.

name: Exchange items on a delivered order
description: Applies when a customer asks to exchange an item from a delivered order for a different variant of the same product and restricts how the price difference must be paid; eligibility, the price difference, and the customer's payment restriction must be verified before submitting or refusing the exchange.
procedure:
- Confirm the order is delivered (pending means modify, not exchange) and verify eligibility: within the product category's exchange window from the delivery date, new variant available and not clearance.
- Compute the price difference as new variant price minus old variant price.
- Honor the customer's payment restriction literally: use only the payment instrument they designated.
- Treat an explicit restriction in the customer's message (e.g., 'only on X', 'do not charge Y') as a standing decline of all other methods — do not ask again or offer alternatives; ask only when the customer named no restriction at all.
- If the designated method's balance is below the difference and the customer has declined alternatives, refuse with the reason that the payment method has insufficient balance; otherwise submit the exchange charged to the designated method.
check: Before refusing for insufficient balance, recompute the price difference from the two variant prices and look up the designated method's current balance: the refusal is valid only if the balance is strictly less than the difference and the customer has restricted payment to that method.
known_bad: A customer designates a gift card with a $50.00 balance for a $27.59 price difference; refusing with insufficient_balance fails the check because the recomputed difference is less than the balance, so the exchange should be submitted instead.

name: Trust the system's recorded refund amount
description: Applies when you compute a refund or charge by hand (e.g., an item price minus a percentage-based fee) and must decide how to round and which figure to report when the system records a different amount after submission.
procedure:
- Compute the expected amount as price × (1 − fee rate) and round half up to the nearest cent; do not truncate the extra decimal.
- Submit the action using the customer's chosen destination and the valid reason.
- Compare the system's recorded amount with your hand computation; if they differ, treat the system's recorded amount as correct.
- Report the system's recorded amount to the customer, noting the withheld fee and its percentage.
check: Recompute the amount with round-half-up to the nearest cent and confirm it matches the system's recorded figure; the figure reported to the customer must equal the recorded figure, not the truncated one.
known_bad: For an item where price × (1 − fee rate) yields a third decimal (e.g., a 10% fee on 111.23 giving 100.107), truncating to 100.10 fails the check because the system records 100.11; reporting the truncated figure is wrong.

name: Resolve ambiguous timestamps for window checks
description: Applies when a policy time window (return, cancellation, exchange) must be checked against dates but the task header gives only a bare numeric timestamp with no units or explicit date.
procedure:
- Read the current date only from the task header's bare numeric timestamp; never adopt a 'today' date from memory or assumption that the environment does not actually state.
- Interpret the bare timestamp relative to the order's dates: as a month/day (M/D) reading that falls near the order's delivery or placement date, or as a day offset from those dates.
- Count the days elapsed since delivery (or placement) using the resolved current date, and compare against the policy window for the product category.
- If plausible interpretations differ, prefer the one consistent with the order record, and refuse for an expired window only if the window is exceeded under every consistent reading.
- When a consistent reading places the request inside the window, proceed with the request even if some other assumed calendar date would put it outside.
check: Recompute the elapsed days under every plausible reading of the header timestamp; if any consistent reading places the request inside the policy window, a refusal with window_expired fails this check.
known_bad: A request on an item delivered a few weeks earlier, with a header timestamp that can be read as a month/day inside the window: treating the timestamp as a far-future calendar date (or an invented 'today') and refusing with window_expired is wrong when the month/day reading is consistent with the order record.
